author: Jaehyun Yeom
message:
Thanks for the comment. The *control flow* is obvious because it only returns at return statement. For example, if I put fmt.Println("something") at line 88, it will print unless the function returns early at line 79. If this was implemented with try, it may return early at try and it's harder to know that quickly.

You're right it depends on the internal error state and that may be hard to understand sometimes. But _basically what scanner does is that it doesn't do anything if it's already done_ (just like bufio.Scanner). That's it.

Does the internal error state give the same complexity? The difference is that try() changes the control flow but method on object is about behavior, and the implementation details are layered.

The out layer, the usage of RespendentScanner is same as bufio.Scanner and I can easily illustrate line 116 to 120 as Example test documentation and it's easy to understand. And that's actually the essence of the rewritten parseRespendents() nothing more than that.

Uncovering another layer, line 77 Scan() function is easy to understand. It just does what it says and early return for done scanner is just like bufio.Scanner.Scan().

One more layer, the parseField() method. Looks a bit verbose but line 48-53 is HandleErrorf, and line 54-57 is just Scan() call, but handling the error properly which was missing in the original code. The rest parsing code is not touched much.

How to read this parseField() code is to see return statements. It has 3 early returns which are indented. One is no-error return early for done scanner, next 2 are error conditions (one is bufio.Scanner error and the other is format error) and error value is set and return. When error happens the scanner is done and further scanning does nothing. That's it. Actually for this case, I may just repeat the defer contents to those 2 error returns just like what I did in parseEmptyLine() method. That's actually one line fewer and easier to read. Just did defer to mimic the original code HandleErrorf() pattern.

We looked all 3 layers. 1st is just a simple for loop, 2nd is just says what it does, 3rd is to return early for done condition and 2 error cases. That's it.

In the original code, because it does return early with try(), we're forced to use defer HandleErrorf(). In the rewritten code, I don't need to depend on defer much. I may copy repeat the code if I think that's cleaner.

You are right that your solution doesn't impact control flow, but only if we're speaking in very strict terms. The internal state of the scanner affects whether the method is going to be executed at all, which I think has a very similar complexity.

I know the article by Rob Pike and I love it :). However, that (and yours) solution has a big shortcoming: you have to reimplement it for everything, it's not reusable.

A gopher will understand `try` once and see it everywhere. With your approach, one has to first understand that specific implementation of the idea from Rob Pike and then proceed.

Also, my code is 2/3 of yours, mostly because I didn't have to implement any architecture for dealing with errors.

I understand your points and admire your code. But I still think `try` is better here and it's complexity in affecting control flow really isn't too much of a complexity.

I think try() is similar to panic() that it can change the control flow without explicit return. If there's a reason not to use panic, I think that's similar for try.

author: Jaehyun Yeom
message:
In most cases, must.Any will be sufficient, it can cover all "one value, one error" cases without much stress. If there are 3 or more return values, it's normally not easy to use it in one line anyway within the expression (not just assignments). There's a way to make it "scale" better, not really difficult to be honest.

I think the reason not to use panic is because it affects control flow and that's why authors of Go teach us that way. In case of runtime errors like divide by zero or index out of bound, it's actually not possible to proceed the logic in the normal control flow structs, so it's unavoidable to use panic. Don't panic means we should minimize that control flow confusion whenever it's possible to avoid that. That's all the background of best practice and so on.

You can test it. I had done and what I found was that it doesn't add that much value. It looks useful in the beginning, but later, I found that there are better ways. It may be useful for some people. Every feature is useful for someone, that's how many languages evolved and became more and more complex. I think Go is very unique, avoiding that mistake.
